title: Chapter 26: I Do Not Wait Anymore
content: The courthouse steps are full at nine on a Tuesday morning, because the paper said nine o'clock and the diner is shut and there is nowhere else in Kestrel Bend to be.
Barrow is waiting at the bottom with an envelope in his glove and a pen already uncapped.
"Miss Aubrey. The District has authorized a settlement of ninety thousand dollars."
He holds out the envelope. Wren does not take it.
"There is a release. Two pages. The check is inside. Sign and it clears today."
"Read it to me."
"I can give you a copy."
"Read it to me. You have it memorized. Men like you always have it memorized."

Barrow's mouth does a small thing. Then he reads. "In consideration of the sum of ninety thousand dollars, the petitioner releases the Basin Authority, its officers, agents and employees, from any and all claims arising from the maintenance event of the twelfth of September 2026, characterized herein as an act of river."
"Act of river."
"That is the phrase."
"Say the rest."
"The petitioner agrees not to publish, file, or cause to be published any further statement concerning the said event."

The steps have gone quiet. There are maybe sixty people on them. Ruthie is at the top with her arms folded and her apron still on. Bram is on the third step with his hands in his pockets. Otis Pell has been brought down in a truck and is standing at the rail with his two sticks.
Wren takes the envelope and holds the check up so the light goes through it. It is pale blue and the amount is printed twice, in figures and in words.
"Ninety thousand dollars," she says. "That is what a man costs when he is not written down."
"Miss Aubrey."
"How much for the others?"
"The offer is in respect of your grandfather."
"I know what it is in respect of. I asked how much for the others."
Barrow says nothing, which is an answer.

"There are forty-one files in a drawer two blocks from here," Wren says. "Every one of them has a widow or a son or a daughter who has been told to come back. Not one of them has been offered a dollar, because a person who is not written down cannot be wronged. That is the whole trick. You cannot sue for a man who does not officially exist."
"That is a legal question."

"It is an arithmetic question. Ninety thousand divided by forty-two is two thousand one hundred and forty-two dollars and eighty-five cents. That is what a life is worth in this county when it is not certified. I have done the division four times."
She takes the pen out of Barrow's hand.
For a second he thinks she is going to sign, and she can see him decide to look relieved too early.

She writes across the first page, in large letters, DECLINED, and under it the date, and under that her initials. Then she takes Junie Hale's stamp out of her coat pocket, breathes on the rubber, and brings it down on the paper.
CERTIFIED.
"There," she says. "Now it is in the record."
Barrow looks at the page. "That is not a notarization."

"It is a stamp. In this town that is the same thing." She folds the release and puts it in his breast pocket. "Take it to her. Tell her the number is wrong. It is not ninety thousand. It is ninety thousand and forty-one."
She goes down the steps past him, and nobody claps, because it is not that kind of town.

At the hardware store on Mill Street she buys a gallon of exterior white oil paint, a two-inch sash brush, a tin of mineral spirits, and a wooden stirrer. The man at the counter reads the label to her.
"Latex will not cure under fifty," he says. "The oil will. It will take two days and it will stink."
"How many letters in a gallon?"
"What kind of letters?"
"Names. Forty-one of them. Two inches high."
"You will need two gallons."
She buys two.

The ferry is up on the slip where the county left it in October, blocked with timber and chained to the bollards, and the fence they put around the landing came down on Sunday night and nobody has put it back up.
Thirty-eight feet of riveted steel, black, with AUBREY'S in white at the bow, gone grey, and a waterline that has been six different heights in her lifetime.
Wren sets the ladder at the bow and puts the stirrer in the can and stirs until her wrist aches, and the paint comes up out of the can the colour of the inside of a shell.
"Read them," she says.
Ruthie stands at the bottom of the ladder with the typed list and her glasses on the end of her nose. "Owen Pike. Fourteenth of May, nineteen ninety-four."
Wren paints it small and level, six inches above the waterline, where a man in a boat would see it. The brush is stiff and the paint is cold and the first letter is bad and she does it again.
"Anna Voss Rusk. Second of August, two thousand and sixteen."
The wind comes up the channel and takes the paint smell downstream.

By the fourth name her hand has found the size, and by the seventh the letters are even, and by the ninth a man has come down the bank with a folding chair and set it up behind her without saying anything.
At eleven it starts to get cold. Bram takes the ladder and moves it. Ruthie reads. Otis Pell stands at the rail with his sticks and does not sit in the chair.
At the fourteenth name a woman comes up the gravel with a boy of about nine.
"That is my father," she says. "Deacon Ross."
"Then you paint him."

She has never held a brush. Wren puts it in her hand and closes her fingers around it and shows her where to start, and the woman paints ROSS in letters that lean, and the boy holds the tin, and nobody says anything for a minute.
After that it becomes a rule. If it is yours, you paint it. If it is not, you hold the light.

By three there are eleven people on the bank, two torches, a thermos going around, and thirty names on the hull. A man from the feed store brings a generator and a lamp on a stand, because the light goes at four thirty now.
Wren leaves the first three feet under the bow clear. She does not say why and nobody asks. Her grandfather has a certificate. A certificate is a thing you can show a bank. The others have this.
At four she is on the ladder at the stern when the clean car comes down the lane and stops outside the fence, and Ottoline Reeve gets out in the grey coat and stands with her hands at her sides.
She looks at the hull for a long time. Then she walks in through the gap where the gate was.
"You are painting county property."
"I am painting names."
"On county property."
"On a boat."
"It is a condemned vessel in a county right of way."
"Then it is a condemned vessel in a county right of way with names on it."
Ottoline's eyes go along the row. Pike. Voss Rusk. Deeds. Ross. Finch. Nunn. She reads them the way she reads a document, left to right, without moving her head.
"I kept their files," she says. "Forty-one folders. Every one of them read. Every one of them in order. Do you think the county did that?"
"You kept copies."

"Nobody else kept anything at all." She says it without heat, which is worse. "In 1994 this district had four staff and a filing cabinet. I have carried those names through six directors and two audits and a federal review, and none of them was ever lost."
"A drawer is not keeping," Wren says. "A drawer is where a thing goes so it does not have to be answered."
"And this is an answer? Paint?"
"It is a list where the water can see it."
Ottoline looks at the paint on Wren's hands.
"In six years the paint will be gone and the file will still be pending."
"Then I will paint it again."
The river goes by. Somewhere behind them Ruthie is telling somebody to keep the light steady.
"As of four o'clock this afternoon," Ottoline says, "I am suspended without pay pending the state's review of permit B-4417."
She says it to the hull, not to Wren.
"The governor's office called at noon. It took four minutes."
"I am sorry."
"No, you are not."
"I am sorry it took a drawer."
Ottoline turns her head then. Her face is tired in a way that has nothing to do with age.

"You think I am the machine," she says. "I am the person who kept the machine running. Forty thousand people have water that does not taste of silt because I signed the schedule. This town has a crossing that does not flood every April because I kept the gate clear. Twenty-two years."
"And my grandfather pulled people out of it for fifty-one."
"Yes," Ottoline says. "He did."
She gets into the car and drives up Ridge Road, slowly, because the road is bad and the car is very clean.

At half past five the light is gone and the lamp on the stand is doing the work. Bram takes the brush at the stern, where the last name goes, and writes his brother's name in letters that are too big, and nobody tells him.
Ade Kessler.
He does not put the date, or the year, or the mile. Wren does not tell him to.
At seven she walks up Third Street with paint on her hands, because the Annex is still open and Hollis Drane is standing in the middle of it.

He has taken the drawer out of the desk and put it on a folding table under the window, and he has taped a sheet of paper to the front of the table that says PHOTOGRAPHS PERMITTED, and a second sheet that says ONE FILE AT A TIME.
There are eleven people in the room. Mars is at the end of the table with her phone, taking pictures for a woman who does not have one.
A woman in a nurse's coat holds a folder open with both hands.
"Nineteen ninety-seven," she says. "That is his handwriting. That is my father's handwriting on the form."
"Then that is yours to photograph," Hollis says.
She does. It takes nine minutes, and nobody hurries her.
"Can I take it?"
"No," Hollis says. "It is the county's copy."
"Then what do I have?"
"A picture," Wren says. "A picture is a copy. A copy is a record. It is the only kind this county has ever honored."
At eight the woman asks Hollis when the files will be certified.
Hollis looks at the drawer and then at the table and then at his own hands.
"Maybe tomorrow," he says.
"No," Wren says. "Not tomorrow. Today."
She takes the folder and photographs every page herself, one after another, and hands the phone back.
"There," she says. "Now there are two, and one of them is not in a drawer."
At nine she goes back down to the landing. The lamp is off. The paint has skinned over and the names are white on the black hull and the frost is already starting at the waterline.
There are boot prints on the deck. One line of them, from the ramp to the rail and back, and they are not hers and they are not Bram's, and they are the only marks on a deck that has been swept.
The badge is clipped to the rail where a passenger puts a hand.

Basin Authority, District 4. T. MARSH, P.E. The photograph is six years old and he has not yet learned to look like an engineer. The clip is sprung, so it has been taken off and put back on a great many times.

Up the hill a truck downshifts on the county road and does not stop at the bend, and she stands in the dark with her hand on the rail where the badge was and counts the gears all the way out of hearing.
highlight: Wren refuses the settlement check, paints the forty-one names on the hull, and leaves Theo's badge on the rail.
